nameStory: Scherffelia is named after botanist Richard Scherffel, an Austrian scientist who studied microscopic algae in the early 1900s. The species name 'dubia' means 'doubtful' in Latin, reflecting the uncertainty scientists had about how to classify this tiny organism when it was first discovered. It's a fitting name for such an elusive and rarely seen species!
description: Scherffelia dubia is actually a microscopic single-celled green alga, not a typical plant that most nature explorers would spot with the naked eye. These tiny organisms form small colonies or live individually in freshwater environments. They're so small you'd need a microscope to see their distinctive features, but they sometimes form thin, greenish films on water surfaces or wet rocks that might catch your attention.

habitat: This microscopic alga lives in freshwater environments throughout New England, including ponds, slow streams, and temporary pools. It prefers nutrient-rich waters and can sometimes be found on wet rocks, soil, or wooden surfaces near water sources. Given its single recorded observation in New England, it's clearly very rare or easily overlooked in our region.

seasonality.spring: Most active during warming weather when freshwater habitats begin to thaw and nutrients become available.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when populations may be large enough to notice as green films on water surfaces.
seasonality.fall: Still present but populations typically declining as temperatures drop and nutrients become scarce.
seasonality.winter: Dormant or present in very small numbers, virtually impossible to detect without laboratory equipment.

funFact: Despite being a single-celled organism, Scherffelia dubia can actually swim using tiny whip-like structures called flagella - imagine a microscopic green torpedo zipping around in a drop of pond water!
confusionNotes: Any green film or scum you see on water is likely other types of algae or cyanobacteria rather than Scherffelia dubia. Without a microscope, it's impossible to distinguish this species from dozens of other microscopic green algae that create similar-looking growths.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that algae like Scherffelia are actually closer relatives to land plants than they are to bacteria, despite their simple appearance. When people talk about 'pond scum' or 'green slime,' they're often looking at communities of thousands of these microscopic plant relatives working together.
compareHints: Since Scherffelia dubia appears to be the only species in its genus found in New England, it's best compared to other microscopic freshwater green algae in different families. Unlike colonial algae that form distinct shapes or filaments, Scherffelia tends to be more loosely organized. Professional identification requires microscopic examination of cell structure and swimming behavior.
